## How this sheet works

Exercises rederive or apply the lecture's results. Do them on your own
time; they are not worked in class.

The class starts open. Discussion 1 is about what you are interested in
or worried about, and nobody is asked how they use AI themselves.
Discussion 2 turns to what could be done: each group is an ethics
committee writing guidelines for the use of AI in one setting, using
ideas from the course. The items under "If there is time" are more
structured, and a class may take one of them up.

A guideline decides who checks, who is told, and who pays when
something goes wrong. So each item ends by asking who bears the cost,
who gains, or who the choice could be justified to.

Notation as in the lecture. A benchmark score is
$\theta + B + \bar\varepsilon$: $\theta$ is what the benchmark is
after, $B$ is the effect of the prompt, judge and settings of one run,
with variance $\tau^2$, and $\bar\varepsilon$ is the average noise over
$n$ items, with variance $\sigma^2 / n$. $\Phi$ is the standard normal
distribution function, and $m_K$ is the expected largest of $K$
independent standard normals.

## Exercises

Attempt each part before you open a hint.

::: {.callout-warning title="Hints"}
Do not open a hint unless you have been stuck for at least a few
minutes, and open them in order.
:::

### Exercise 1. Fixed or random

A benchmark has $n$ items, and a model answers about 80% of them
correctly, so $\sigma^2 = 0.8 \times 0.2 = 0.16$. Each run uses one
prompt and one judge, and the choice of these moves the score with
standard deviation $\tau = 0.03$, that is, 3 points.

(a) With $n = 100$, find the naive standard error, the true standard
error when the target is $\theta$, and the probability that the naive
95% interval contains $\theta$.

(b) Repeat for $n = 400$.

(c) A lab runs the 400 items under $J$ different, equally reasonable
setups and averages the $J$ scores. How large must $J$ be for the
standard error of the average to be at most 2 points?

(d) A lab can publish the interval from (b) or the one from (c). Who
gains from the narrower one being published, and who is misled by it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
For (a): the naive standard error is $\sigma / \sqrt n$, the true one
$\sqrt{\sigma^2 / n + \tau^2}$, and the coverage is
$2\,\Phi(1.96\, r) - 1$ with $r$ their ratio.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 2"}
For (c): each setup draws its own $B$, so the average of $J$ runs has
variance $(\sigma^2 / n + \tau^2) / J$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) Naive: $\sqrt{0.16 / 100} = 0.04$. True:
$\sqrt{0.0016 + 0.0009} = 0.05$. So $r = 0.8$ and the coverage is
$2\,\Phi(1.57) - 1 = 88\%$.

(b) Naive: $\sqrt{0.16 / 400} = 0.02$. True:
$\sqrt{0.0004 + 0.0009} = 0.036$. So $r = 0.555$ and the coverage is
$2\,\Phi(1.09) - 1 = 72\%$. Four times the items halved the reported
interval and lowered its coverage.

(c) The variance of the average is $0.0013 / J$, which is at most
$0.02^2 = 0.0004$ when $J \ge 3.25$. Four setups give a standard error
of $\sqrt{0.0013 / 4} = 0.018$.

(d) The lab gains: a narrow interval makes a small lead over a rival
look settled. People who choose a model by the comparison are misled,
and so is a rival whose equally good model appears to be behind. The
interval in (c) costs four times the computing and has to be reported
as wider than a competitor's naive one, so a lab that reports it looks
worse unless everyone does.
:::

### Exercise 2. The best of $K$

On a leaderboard, the score of one version of a model has noise with
standard deviation $\sigma = 8$ Elo. Use $m_{10} = 1.54$.

(a) A lab tests 10 private versions that are in truth equally good and
publishes the best. By how much does the published score overstate, on
average?

(b) Lab A tests 27 equally good versions and publishes the best. Lab B
tests one. The two labs' models are in truth equally good, with the
same noise. Find the probability that A's published score is above
B's.

(c) After publication, three fresh votes arrive for each vote from the
testing period. Treating the score as an average over votes, how much
of the overstatement in (a) remains?

(d) Who pays for the rank in (b)?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
For (b): there are 28 scores with the same distribution. Which one is
the largest?
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) $\sigma\, m_{10} = 8 \times 1.54 = 12.3$ Elo.

(b) All 28 scores are independent draws from one distribution, so each
is equally likely to be the largest. A's published score is above B's
when the largest is one of A's 27: probability $27/28 = 96\%$.

(c) A quarter of the score's weight is on the old votes, so about
$12.3 / 4 = 3.1$ Elo remains. A leaderboard's rating is not a plain
average, so this gives the direction and the rough size.

(d) Lab B, which is ranked below an equally good model for testing one
version, and anyone who chooses a model by the rank. Testing many
private versions takes resources, so the practice favors the largest
providers.
:::

### Exercise 3. New items

Invented numbers. A model answers 86% of the 1,200 problems in a public
benchmark correctly. Researchers write 1,200 new problems by the same
recipe, and people find them as hard as the old ones. The model answers
78% of the new problems correctly.

(a) Find the difference, its standard error and a 95% interval.
Could chance explain the difference?

(b) Give two explanations other than chance. What would you measure to
tell them apart?

(c) In the lecture's graph of the paths into a score, which arrow does
the difference estimate?

(d) Who gains when 86% is the number reported?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
For (a): the two sets of problems are separate samples, so the
variances of the two proportions add.
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) The difference is 8 points. Its standard error is
$\sqrt{0.86 \times 0.14 / 1200 + 0.78 \times 0.22 / 1200} = 0.0156$,
about 1.6 points, so the interval is 8 plus or minus 3.1: from 4.9 to
11.1 points. The difference is about 5 standard errors, so chance does
not explain it.

(b) The new problems could be harder for models in a way that people
do not notice. Or the model could have been exposed to the old
problems, or tuned to problems like them. If the new problems were
harder, every model should score lower on them, including models
released before the benchmark was published. If exposure is the cause,
the difference should be larger for models that can reproduce the old
problems word for word, and absent for models trained before the
benchmark existed.

(c) The arrow from tuning to the benchmark into the score. New, unseen
items cut that arrow and leave capability's arrow in place, so under
the second explanation the 78% is the better estimate of what the
model does on problems of this kind.

(d) The developer, whose model looks 8 points better than it is on
problems it has not seen. People who rely on the model for new
problems are the ones misled.
:::

### Exercise 4. Two averages

Requesters post paid tasks on a platform, and workers do them. Invented
numbers: nine requesters pay \$12 an hour and post 1 hour of work each;
one requester pays \$1 an hour and posts 91 hours.

(a) Find the average hourly rate over requesters, and the average over
hours of work.

(b) Hara et al. (2018) found, in the logs of 2,676 workers on Amazon
Mechanical Turk, that the average requester paid more than \$11 an hour
and the median worker earned about \$2 an hour. Give two reasons the
numbers can both be right.

(c) Which average would the platform quote, and whose experience does
each one describe?

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) Over requesters: $(9 \times 12 + 1 \times 1) / 10 = 10.90$. Over
hours: $(9 \times 12 + 91 \times 1) / 100 = 1.99$.

(b) The two are averages with different weights: each requester
counted once, or each counted by the work posted, and the authors
report that lower-paying requesters post much more work. A worker's
hour also includes time no requester pays for, such as searching for
tasks and work that is rejected. (One number is also a mean and the
other a median.)

(c) The platform would quote the average over requesters, which
describes what a typical customer pays. The average over hours
describes what an hour of a worker's time earns. Both are true, and a
report that gives only the first has chosen who to describe.
:::

## In class

### Discussion 1: open floor

What about AI are you most interested in, or most worried about?

Nobody is asked how they use AI themselves.

1. Alone, for a minute: write down one thing.
2. In pairs, for two minutes: what did each of you write, and why that
   one?
3. With the room: what are the themes?
4. For one theme: who bears the cost if the worry comes true, and who
   is in a position to prevent it?

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Some directions" collapse="true"}
There are no right answers here. Themes that often come up, with where
the course has met them:

- Learning and skills: deskilling, and the chatbot in a maths class
  (grades up with it, exam scores down without it).
- Jobs and pay: who benefits, and the survey in which executives
  report little change so far.
- Trust: sycophancy, deepfakes, undisclosed AI in political ads.
- Fairness: whose writing and labeling the systems are built from.
- Hype: benchmarks, and what a score does and does not show.
- The environment: small in aggregate, large near one plant.
- Responsibility: someone gave the instructions, and someone answers
  for them.

On question 4, the people who bear a cost are often not the ones who
can prevent it. That gap is what a guideline is for.
:::

### Discussion 2: an ethics committee

First, for two or three of the themes: what would have to be true for
this worry to be smaller? Who could make it true?

Then each group is the ethics committee of one of these, a different
one from every other group:

- a university, for teaching and assessment;
- an employer, such as a bank or a consultancy;
- a government department that decides on benefits or visas;
- a hospital;
- a newsroom.

The committee has been asked for guidelines on the use of AI. Write at
most five. Each should be a condition that someone could check.

Your guidelines should answer these:

1. What is the AI for here, and how would you know it works in this
   setting, and not only on a benchmark?
2. Who checks its output, and who signs?
3. What is disclosed, and to whom?
4. Who bears the errors? Whose work was it built from?
5. Once the guideline exists, how will people get around it?
6. Who can say no?

Then swap with another committee. Read their guidelines as someone the
guidelines would hurt, or as someone who wants to get around them.
Which guideline fails first, and who does the failure fall on?

Last, each committee keeps one guideline. Who would it have to be
justified to?

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Some directions" collapse="true"}
Ideas from the course behind each question:

1. Validity. A score on a benchmark is not performance on the tasks in
   use here; a trial in the setting, with the outcome that counts
   there, is the evidence. Goal selection: what is being optimized,
   speed, cost or quality, and for who?
2. Levels of abstraction: the tool executes instructions, and a person
   answers for them. A named person signs, and has the time and the
   skill to check. A signature without those makes the signer the one
   who takes the blame for a system they could not control.
3. Honest reporting: say where AI was used and what was checked, as
   the revised Deloitte report did only after its errors were found.
   Disclosure to the person affected differs from disclosure to a
   regulator.
4. Justice: errors fall on applicants, patients, students or readers,
   who did not choose the tool. Upstream are the people whose writing
   and labeling built it.
5. Goodhart's law: a rule that counts something checkable (a
   disclosure box ticked, a detector's score) will be met on paper.
   Ask what the rule's measure stops measuring once people aim at it.
6. Leverage: whether a person can ask for a human decision, and
   whether staff can decline to use the tool without penalty.

A guideline such as "AI must be used responsibly" cannot be checked.
"Every decision letter names the person who reviewed it" can.
:::

## If there is time

### Problem 1. Did AI deskill the endoscopists?

In a colonoscopy, the adenoma detection rate is the share of procedures
in which the doctor finds at least one precancerous growth. At four
centers in Poland, AI assistance was introduced for some procedures.
Among procedures done without AI, doctors found an adenoma in 226 of
795 in the three months before AI was introduced, and in 145 of 648 in
the three months after (Budzyń et al., 2025).

(a) Find the two detection rates, their difference and a 95% interval
for it.

(b) Draw a graph with the period (before or after), the doctors' skill
and detection, and add whatever else could differ between the two
periods. Which paths from period to detection do not go through
skill?

(c) In Norway, doctors used AI for a period and it was then withdrawn,
by design. Among inexperienced doctors, the odds ratio for detection
after withdrawal against the period before AI was 1.03, with a 95%
interval from 0.79 to 1.34 (Pedersen et al., 2026). What does this
design hold fixed that the first does not? Does the study show that
there is no deskilling?

(d) A hospital has to decide now whether to keep the AI. Who bears the
error if it keeps the AI and deskilling is real? Who bears it if it
withdraws the AI and deskilling is not real?

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Hint 1"}
For (a): a difference of two proportions from separate samples.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .answer collapse="true" title="Hint 2"}
For (b): once AI is available, who decides which procedures are done
without it?
:::

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Solution" collapse="true"}
(a) $226 / 795 = 28.4\%$ and $145 / 648 = 22.4\%$, a difference of 6.0
points. The standard error is
$\sqrt{0.284 \times 0.716 / 795 + 0.224 \times 0.776 / 648} = 0.023$,
so the interval is from 1.6 to 10.5 points, as the paper reports.

(b) Period → AI available → skill → detection is the deskilling path.
Others: period → patients → detection, if the patients or the reasons
for their procedures changed; period → which procedures are done
without AI → detection, since after AI arrives the procedures without
it are a selected set, perhaps the ones expected to be simple; and
period → workload, staffing or equipment → detection. The comparison
conditions on "done without AI", which means something different in
the two periods. A before-and-after comparison cannot separate these
paths.

(c) The same doctors are followed, and the withdrawal is set by the
study and not chosen case by case, so "without AI" after the
withdrawal is every procedure and not a selected set. The interval
includes 1, and it also includes odds 21% lower, so the study does not
show a loss of skill and does not rule a moderate one out. Its outcome
(polyps of at least 5 mm) and its setting differ from the first
study's. The claim is contested.

(d) If the AI stays and deskilling is real, the cost falls on patients
whose procedures are done without it, on days it is unavailable or at
centers that do not have it, and on the doctors, whose skill is
theirs to lose. If the AI is withdrawn and deskilling is not real,
patients lose the detections the AI adds: in Norway, inexperienced
doctors found more with it. Patients bear both errors, and they are
not the ones who decide.
:::

### Discussion 3: who answers for it?

In the lecture: the computer is executing instructions; someone gave
them, and someone answers for them. Each group takes a different case.

- A consulting firm delivers a report to a government department with
  a fabricated quotation and references to research that does not
  exist (McGuirk, 2025).
- A woman with epilepsy stops her medication on a schedule that, her
  parents' lawsuit alleges, a chatbot drew up, and dies (Ottilie,
  2026).
- A campaign runs an ad with an AI-generated video of its opponent
  (Brumfiel, 2026).
- Workers at an outsourcing firm label violent and sexual content for
  an AI company, for about \$2 an hour (Stahl, 2024).

1. Who gave the instructions?
2. Who could have checked, and did they have the time and the skill?
3. Who was harmed?
4. Who is likely to be blamed? Is that the person who had control?

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Some directions" collapse="true"}
The report: staff wrote the request and accepted the output, and
partners signed. The firm agreed to repay part of its fee. The
department's readers were harmed, and so were the people the report
was about. The medical advice: the user asked, and a company chose
what the product would say and how agreeable it would be; the case is
an allegation and has not been decided. The idea that someone gave the
instructions is hardest to apply here, since the person who typed the
request is the person harmed. The ad: a campaign commissioned it;
viewers and the opponent are harmed, and a disclosure rule would move
the check to the broadcaster or the platform. The labeling: the AI
company wrote the contract and the outsourcing firm set the pay and
the targets; each can point to the other.

On question 4: blame tends to fall on the person nearest the system,
who may have had the least control over it. The reading calls this a
moral crumple zone.
:::

### Discussion 4: you sign the report

In the lecture you wrote, alone, what you owe the reader before you
sign a report whose data cleaning, model and first draft a tool chose.

1. Compare what you wrote. What did someone else have that you did
   not?
2. Write a disclosure for the report, in at most three sentences.
3. One group reads theirs. What could a reader still not know?
4. What do you owe the reader, and why?

::: {.callout-note .answer title="Some directions" collapse="true"}
A disclosure can say what the tool did (chose the cleaning steps and
the model, wrote the draft), what the analyst checked (reran the
analysis, compared with another specification, read every reference)
and what was not checked. Honest reporting: which of the analyses the
tool tried is the one reported? Ownership: the signature says the
analyst chose, so the analyst has to be able to defend each choice the
tool made, or say that they cannot.
:::
